steps.title: Why a message needs a seal
text: A lock hides a message, but a listener can still change it. A seal lets the receiver see that a message changed.
This lesson builds four seals, from weak to strong. Each one adds an idea that the last one lacked.
A seal can also show who sent a message, when only two people hold the key. You will see where that proof stops.
Built to show the parts. Do not copy.

steps.title: A fingerprint for data
text: A {{term:hash}} turns any message into a fixed-size fingerprint. SHA-256 gives 32 bytes, which is 256 bits.
The diagram shows the fingerprint of a message beside the fingerprint after one bit flip. Each cell is one bit, and it lights up when the two differ.
About half the cells light up. One tiny edit scrambles the whole fingerprint, so even a small edit is easy to spot.

steps.title: A hash alone proves little
text: The first seal is a plain hash of the message. The receiver hashes the message again and compares the two fingerprints.
Try it: flip a bit in the message. The old seal no longer fits, and the compare fails.
A real attacker would also recompute the hash, because no secret is involved. A plain hash catches accidents only.

tryIt.label: Flip a bit in the message

steps.title: Add a secret key
text: The second seal puts a secret {{term:key}} in front of the message before hashing. Only the two sides know the key.
A plain edit now fails, because the attacker cannot rebuild the seal without the key. The next step shows a trick that still gets through.

steps.title: The trick that forges a seal
text: Try it: add text to the end of the message and forge a new seal with no key. Press the button.
The server accepts it. The check passed, and that pass is the lesson.
SHA-256 reads a message in chunks, and its output shows where it stopped. An attacker can restart from that point and add more text. This is a length extension attack.

tryIt.label: Extend the message and forge the seal

claims.text: SHA-256 pads a message with a 1 bit, zeros and a 64-bit length, then processes the blocks in order, each starting from the previous hash value. The final digest is therefore the starting state for any further blocks. In the lab, a forged seal for the message plus extra text passes the keyed-hash compare.
claims.source: FIPS 180-4, sections 5.1.1 (padding) and 6.2.2 (SHA-256 hash computation); the attack's name appears in FIPS 202, Appendix A.1; lab result: docs/lessons-1-3-names.md, Lesson 2 attacks, L2-extend-keyed-hash

steps.title: HMAC closes the gap
text: {{term:hmac}} hashes twice and mixes the key in at both ends. The inner hash sits inside an outer hash, and the lab shows the restart trick fail.
Try it: run the same forgery against the HMAC message. The check named HMAC compare fails.

claims.text: HMAC is H((K xor opad) || H((K xor ipad) || message)), a nested hash.
In the lab, the same extension forgery against the HMAC message is rejected by the check named HMAC compare, with code SEAL_HMAC_MISMATCH.

steps.title: Any flip breaks the seal
text: A flipped bit in the message breaks the HMAC. A flipped bit in the seal breaks it too.
Try it: flip a bit in the seal field. The compare fails, and the server drops the message.

tryIt.label: Flip a bit in the HMAC seal

steps.title: CMAC does the same job with AES
text: {{term:cmac}} makes a seal from a block cipher such as AES instead of a hash. It suits a device that already has AES and little room for more code.
Try it: flip a bit in the message. The check named CMAC compare fails.

tryIt.label: Flip a bit in the CMAC message

claims.text: CMAC is a message authentication code built from a block cipher such as AES.
claims.source: NIST SP 800-38B, section 3 (Introduction: a MAC algorithm based on a symmetric key block cipher) and section 6.2 (MAC generation)

steps.title: Who made the seal?
text: All four seals passed on the normal run. A passing seal tells the receiver two things: the message is unchanged, and the sender held the key.
It cannot tell which key holder sent it. The client and the server share one key, so either one could have made the seal.
To prove to a third party who signed something, you need a signature. Lesson 4 covers signatures and certificates.

claims.text: A MAC made with a shared key shows that the sender held the key, and gives no proof to a third party of which key holder made it.
claims.source: NIST SP 800-175B Rev. 1, section on message authentication (a MAC offers no non-repudiation)

steps.title: What to take away
text: A plain hash catches accidents. A keyed hash stops simple edits but falls to length extension.
HMAC and CMAC are the sound seals. Use a real library for them in any real program.
Built to show the parts. Do not copy.
